About

The person behind the camera

I started on film sets as the person who translates — a fixer with a phrasebook, hired because I knew which grandfather in which village would talk. After three years of translating other people’s questions, I bought a camera and started asking my own.

My first film followed Lisbon’s last tram drivers through one winter of 4 a.m. starts. It was shot on a borrowed camera and edited on a laptop that overheated twice a day — and it taught me the only rule I still work by: stay longer than feels polite, and the real film starts.

Since then: 34 films, nine countries, one small camera kit carried by hand. I work solo or with a crew of two, I record my own sound, and I subtitle everything myself in Portuguese, English and German. If that sounds slow, it is. It is also why clients keep the films for years.

Questions

Before you ask

Do you travel for commissions?

Constantly. Lisbon is home, but nine of the last eleven productions were shot elsewhere in Europe. Travel days are billed at half the shooting rate, and she travels light — one kit, no freight.

Who owns the footage?

You do — the finished film and the project archive transfer to you on final payment. Mara keeps only the right to show excerpts in this portfolio.

How fast is the edit?

A brand film is usually cut within three weeks of the last shooting day. Documentaries take as long as they take — with a viewing copy every fortnight, so you are never left guessing.

Which languages do you work in?

Interviews and direction in Portuguese, English and German. Subtitles in all three are done by Mara herself, never farmed out.

How does booking work?

A signed one-page agreement and a 30% deposit hold your dates. The balance is due on delivery of the viewing copy — no surprises: the calculator on this page is the real rate card.
